title: The sunk cost fallacy
context: Listen to part of a talk in an economics class.

lines.t: Today's topic is something economists call the sunk cost fallacy. A sunk cost is money, time or effort that you've already spent and can't get back. Standard economic theory says that sunk costs should be ignored. The only question that matters for a decision is what happens from now on. Yet people find this extremely hard to do.

A classic demonstration involved theater season tickets. Researchers sold tickets to some buyers at the full price and gave others an unexpected discount. In the first half of the season, the people who'd paid full price went to noticeably more plays, even though the money was equally gone for everyone. They seemed to feel they had to get their money's worth.

The fallacy shows up on a much larger scale, too. The British and French governments kept funding the Concorde jet long after it was clear it would never pay back its development costs, and the error is sometimes even called the Concorde fallacy. Incidentally, I flew on Concorde once as a student, a rare treat, and I can tell you the seats were surprisingly cramped. Anyway.

Now, I don't want to suggest that sticking with a costly project is always irrational. If abandoning it would damage your reputation, or if you'd learn something valuable by finishing it, those are future benefits, not sunk costs, and it's perfectly sensible to weigh them. The mistake happens only when the money already spent becomes the reason itself.

title: Fungal networks beneath the forest
context: Listen to part of a talk in a botany class.

lines.t: Let's turn to what's happening underground. The large majority of land plants, by most estimates around eighty to ninety percent of species, form partnerships with fungi called mycorrhizae. The fungus wraps around or even grows into the plant's roots, and its thin threads spread through the soil far beyond where the roots could reach. The fungus collects water and nutrients, especially phosphorus, and passes them to the plant. In return, the plant feeds the fungus sugars it makes through photosynthesis.

Because one fungus can connect to several plants, scientists started talking about networks linking whole forests. In the late nineteen nineties, a study in Canada used carbon tracers and found that carbon moved between birch and fir trees, apparently through these fungal links. The press loved it and called it the wood wide web.
So is it true that big old trees feed their seedlings through the network?

That's the popular version, the so-called mother tree idea, and I'd be careful with it. A review published in twenty twenty-three looked at the field studies and concluded that the evidence for trees sending resources to their own offspring is weak. Carbon can move, but often in tiny amounts, and it's hard to rule out other routes, like through the soil itself. So the partnership between a plant and its fungus is very well established. The forest-wide sharing story is much less so.

title: The Little Ice Age
context: Listen to part of a talk in a climate history class.

lines.t: Between roughly the fourteenth and the mid nineteenth centuries, much of the Northern Hemisphere went through a cooler period that we call the Little Ice Age. I should say right away that the name is a bit misleading. It wasn't an ice age at all. Average temperatures probably fell by less than one degree, and the cooling wasn't the same everywhere or at the same time. But even a small drop in the average meant shorter growing seasons, failed harvests and glaciers advancing in the Alps.

What caused it? Two factors stand out. One was volcanic activity. Large eruptions throw particles high into the atmosphere, where they reflect sunlight. The eruption of Tambora in Indonesia in eighteen fifteen led to what people in Europe and North America called the year without a summer, with snow in June in New England. The other factor was a period of low solar activity, when astronomers observed hardly any sunspots.

You've probably seen paintings of frost fairs on the River Thames in London, with people skating and setting up stalls on the ice, and they're often used as proof of how cold it was. But the river froze partly because of the old London Bridge. Its many narrow arches slowed the water down, which made it easier to freeze. When the bridge was replaced in the eighteen thirties, the river ran faster, and it hasn't frozen over in central London since.

title: Writing began with bookkeeping
context: Listen to part of a talk in an archaeology class.

lines.t: When we think of the invention of writing, we tend to imagine poetry, laws or history. But in Mesopotamia, in what's now Iraq, the earliest writing we have, from the city of Uruk over five thousand years ago, is almost entirely about bookkeeping. These clay tablets record things like rations of barley given to workers, numbers of sheep, quantities of beer. Writing seems to have started as a tool for managing an economy run by temples and officials.

There's an influential theory about how this happened. For thousands of years before writing, people in the region used small clay tokens of different shapes, a cone for a measure of grain, perhaps, or a cylinder for an animal. Sometimes these tokens were sealed inside hollow clay balls, a kind of envelope, so a shipment couldn't be tampered with. To show what was inside without breaking the ball, people pressed the tokens into its surface. And at some point, the argument goes, they realized the marks alone were enough.
So the tokens just disappeared?

Gradually, yes. Flat tablets replaced the envelopes, and the signs became more abstract, made by pressing a cut reed into wet clay, which gives the wedge shapes that cuneiform is named after. I'll admit that not every scholar accepts the token theory, since the link between particular tokens and particular signs isn't always clear. But the basic point holds. Literature came centuries later.

title: Where the elements come from
context: Listen to part of a talk in an astronomy class.

lines.t: Where did the atoms in your body come from? The Big Bang produced almost nothing but hydrogen and helium, plus a tiny trace of lithium. Everything else, the carbon in your cells, the oxygen you breathe, the calcium in your bones, had to be made later, inside stars.

A star like the Sun spends most of its life fusing hydrogen into helium in its core. Late in life, it can fuse helium into carbon and oxygen. Stars much more massive than the Sun go further, building heavier and heavier elements in layers, a bit like an onion, until they reach iron. And iron is where it stops. Fusing lighter elements releases energy, but fusing iron consumes energy. So once the core fills with iron, the star can no longer support itself. The core collapses, and the outer layers are blasted into space in a supernova, spreading those elements through the galaxy.

What about elements heavier than iron, like gold? These are built mainly when atomic nuclei capture neutrons very quickly. For a long time, supernovas were assumed to be the main source. Then, in twenty seventeen, astronomers detected gravitational waves from two neutron stars colliding, and telescopes saw the glow of freshly made heavy elements. Many astronomers now think collisions like that produce much of the universe's gold. So the ring on your finger may be the debris of a crash between two dead stars.

title: Caravaggio and the drama of light
context: Listen to part of a talk in an art history class.

lines.t: Today, Caravaggio, the Italian painter who worked mainly in Rome around sixteen hundred. His most recognizable feature is his use of light. Many painters used contrasts of light and shadow, but Caravaggio pushed it to an extreme. His figures often emerge from almost total darkness, lit by a single strong beam, as though someone had switched on a spotlight. Art historians call this extreme version tenebrism, from an Italian word for darkness.

Look at The Calling of Saint Matthew. A beam of light enters from the right, following the gesture of Christ's hand, and falls on a group of tax collectors sitting at a table. The light isn't just decoration. It tells the story, showing the moment Matthew is chosen. And notice the people. They look like ordinary Romans in contemporary clothes, because Caravaggio used people from the street as models, which shocked some critics who thought religious figures should look idealized.

Now, Caravaggio's life was famously violent. He was arrested repeatedly, and in sixteen oh six he killed a man and had to flee Rome. It's tempting to read his dark paintings as a reflection of a dark personality, and a lot of popular books do exactly that. I'd resist it. His style was fully developed before the worst of his troubles, and it was a deliberate artistic strategy that dozens of painters across Europe soon copied.

title: Comparative advantage
context: Listen to part of a talk in an economics class.

lines.t: Today's idea is one of the most important, and most misunderstood, in economics: comparative advantage. It was set out by David Ricardo in eighteen seventeen. Let me start with a simple example. Imagine a lawyer who also happens to type faster than her assistant. Should she do her own typing? Probably not. Every hour she spends typing is an hour she isn't spending on legal work, which earns far more. Even though she's better at both tasks, it pays for her to focus on the one where her advantage is greatest and let the assistant type.
But with countries, if one country is better at producing everything, why would it trade at all?

That's exactly the case Ricardo was interested in. In his example, Portugal could produce both wine and cloth with less labor than England. But Portugal's advantage was much bigger in wine. So if Portugal specialized in wine and England in cloth, and they traded, both could end up with more of both goods than if each produced everything itself. What matters isn't absolute ability, it's what you give up, the opportunity cost.

Now, I want to add a caution, because this theory is sometimes used to claim that trade benefits everyone. It shows that a country as a whole can gain. It doesn't say that every worker gains. An English wine maker would be out of a job. How those gains and losses are shared is a political question the model doesn't answer.

title: Giants and dwarfs on islands
context: Listen to part of a talk in an evolutionary biology class.

lines.t: Islands are natural laboratories for evolution, and one of the strangest patterns they show is a change in body size. Biologists call it the island rule. Large mammals that become isolated on islands tend to shrink over many generations, while small animals tend to grow larger.

Some of the best examples are fossil elephants. On Mediterranean islands such as Sicily and Malta, elephants evolved into dwarf forms, some only about a meter tall at the shoulder. On the Indonesian island of Flores, there were dwarf relatives of elephants too, and, in the same place, giant rats several times the size of a common rat. The usual explanation goes like this. On a small island, food is limited, so a big animal that needs less food has an advantage. Small animals, on the other hand, often find themselves with fewer predators and fewer competitors, so being larger becomes possible and even useful.

Flores is also where researchers found Homo floresiensis, a small human species, about a meter tall, and some scientists have suggested its size is another case of island dwarfing. That's still debated, by the way, because we don't know for certain which larger ancestor it came from.

I should also warn you that the rule is a tendency, not a law. When researchers have analyzed large data sets, they've found plenty of exceptions, and some argue the pattern is weaker than textbooks suggest.

title: Thawing permafrost
context: Listen to part of a talk in an earth science class.

lines.t: Permafrost is ground that has stayed frozen for at least two years in a row, and in places like Siberia, Alaska and northern Canada, some of it has been frozen for many thousands of years. It holds a huge amount of carbon, the remains of plants and animals that died long ago but never fully decomposed, because the cold slowed down the microbes that would normally break them down. Current estimates suggest permafrost soils contain roughly twice as much carbon as the atmosphere does today.

Here's the problem. As the Arctic warms, which it's doing much faster than the global average, permafrost thaws, and those microbes wake up. Where the thawed ground is fairly dry, they release carbon dioxide. Where it's waterlogged, without much oxygen, they produce methane, which traps far more heat than carbon dioxide over the first few decades. And more greenhouse gas means more warming, which means more thaw. That's what we call a feedback loop.

In some places thaw is gradual, just a few centimeters deeper each summer. In others, ice-rich ground collapses suddenly, forming new lakes and sinkholes, which exposes deep carbon much faster. You'll sometimes read headlines about a carbon bomb that's ready to explode. Personally, I think that's the wrong picture. The evidence suggests a steady release over decades and centuries, which is serious, but it means that what we do about emissions now still makes a difference.

title: Rewriting memories
context: Listen to part of a talk in a neuroscience class.

lines.t: For most of the twentieth century, the standard view was that once a memory is consolidated, meaning stored in a stable long-term form, it stays more or less fixed. Recalling it was like taking a file out of a cabinet, reading it, and putting it back unchanged.

In two thousand, a study with rats challenged that view. The rats learned to associate a tone with a mild electric shock, so they froze whenever they heard the tone. Later, the researchers played the tone again, which reactivated the memory, and immediately injected a drug that blocks the production of new proteins in the part of the brain involved in fear. Afterwards, the rats behaved as if they'd forgotten the association. The same drug had no effect if the memory wasn't reactivated first.
So remembering something actually makes it fragile?

That's the idea. When a memory is recalled, it seems to become unstable for a while and has to be stored again, which is why it's called reconsolidation. It also fits nicely with research on eyewitnesses, who can absorb misleading details when they're questioned. Each time you retell a story, you may be slightly rewriting it.

Naturally, clinicians got excited. Could you weaken traumatic memories this way? Some trials with people suffering from post-traumatic stress have tried pairing recall with a medication, and the results so far are mixed. I find the basic science convincing, but I'd want much more evidence before calling it a treatment.
